title: IV. Cana Of Galilee
paragraphs: By monastery standards it was very late when Alyosha got back to the hermitage, and the doorkeeper let him in through a side entrance. Nine o’clock had struck, the hour for rest and quiet after a day that had shaken everyone. Alyosha opened the door timidly and went into the elder’s cell, where the coffin now stood. Nobody was there except Father Païssy, who was reading the Gospel alone beside the coffin, and the young novice Porfiry. Porfiry was exhausted by the previous night’s talk and the day’s disturbing events, and he lay in the other room, sleeping the deep, sound sleep of youth on the floor. Father Païssy heard Alyosha come in but did not even look up. Alyosha turned right from the door, went to the corner, dropped to his knees and began to pray.

His soul was full to overflowing, but with mixed feelings. No one feeling stood out clearly; each pushed out the one before it in a slow, steady rotation. Still, there was a sweetness in his heart, and, strangely, Alyosha was not surprised by it. Once again he saw the coffin in front of him, with the hidden dead man so dear to him inside. But the tears and sharp grief of the morning no longer ached in him. As soon as he had come in, he had thrown himself down before the coffin as before a holy shrine, and yet joy, joy was glowing in his mind and heart. The cell’s one window stood open, and the air was cool and fresh. “So the smell must have got worse, if they’ve opened the window,” thought Alyosha. But even the thought of that smell of decay, which only a few hours ago had seemed so dreadful and so humiliating, no longer made him miserable or angry. He began praying quietly, but soon noticed he was praying almost mechanically. Scraps of thought drifted through his soul, flashed like stars and went out again, and others took their place. Yet a feeling of the wholeness of things ruled in his soul, something steady and comforting, and he was aware of it himself. At times he began to pray with fervor; he longed to pour out his thanks and his love....

But no sooner had he begun to pray than he would slip off to something else and fall into thought, forgetting both the prayer and whatever had broken it off. He started to listen to what Father Païssy was reading, but he was worn out, and little by little he began to doze.
“_And the third day there was a marriage in Cana of Galilee,_” read Father Païssy. “_And the mother of Jesus was there. And Jesus was called to the marriage, and his disciples with him._”

“A marriage? What’s that?... A marriage!” whirled through Alyosha’s mind. “There’s happiness for her, too.... She’s gone to the feast.... No, she didn’t take the knife.... That was just a tragic phrase.... Well ... tragic phrases should be forgiven; they have to be. They comfort the heart.... Without them, grief would be too heavy for anyone to bear. Rakitin has gone off down the back alley. As long as Rakitin keeps brooding over his grievances, he will always go off down the back alley.... But the high road ... the road is wide and straight and bright as crystal, with the sun at the end of it.... Ah!... What is being read?”...
“_And when they ran out of wine, the mother of Jesus said to him, They have no wine_” ... Alyosha heard.

“Ah, yes, I was missing this, and I didn’t want to miss it; I love this passage. It’s Cana of Galilee, the first miracle.... Ah, that miracle! That sweet miracle! It wasn’t men’s grief that Christ visited but their joy. He worked His first miracle to help people’s gladness.... ‘Whoever loves men loves their gladness, too’ ... He used to repeat that all the time; it was one of his leading ideas.... ‘There’s no living without joy,’ Mitya says.... Yes, Mitya.... ‘Everything true and good is always full of forgiveness,’ he used to say that, too” ...
“_Jesus said to her, Woman, what has it to do with you or me? Mine hour is not yet come._
“_His mother said to the servants, Whatever he tells you, do it_” ...

“Do it.... The gladness of some poor people, very poor people.... Of course they were poor, if they hadn’t even enough wine for a wedding.... The historians write that the people living around the Lake of Gennesaret in those days were the poorest you could possibly imagine ... and another great heart, that other great being, His Mother, knew that He hadn’t come only to make His great and terrible sacrifice. She knew His heart was open even to the simple, artless merrymaking of some obscure, uneducated people who had warmly asked Him to their poor wedding. ‘Mine hour is not yet come,’ He said with a gentle smile (He must have smiled gently to her). And really, was it to supply wine at poor people’s weddings that He had come down to earth? And yet He went and did what she asked.... Ah, he’s reading again”....
“_Jesus said to them, Fill the waterpots with water. And they filled them to the brim._
“_And he said to them, Now draw some out and take it to the governor of the feast. And they took it._

“_When the ruler of the feast tasted the water that had become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the governor of the feast called the bridegroom,_
“_And said to him, Every man serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, the worse; but you have kept the good wine until now._”

“But what is this, what is this? Why is the room getting wider?... Ah, yes ... it’s the marriage, the wedding ... yes, of course. There are the guests, there sit the young couple, and the merry crowd, and ... Where is the wise governor of the feast? But who is that? Who? The walls are moving back again.... Who is getting up from the great table over there? What!... He, here too? But he’s in the coffin ... and yet he’s here, too. He has stood up, he sees me, he’s coming this way.... God!”...

Yes, he came over to him, to him—the little, thin old man, his face lined with tiny wrinkles, glad and laughing softly. The coffin was gone, and he was dressed as he had been yesterday, when he sat with them and the visitors gathered around him. His face was uncovered, and his eyes were shining. How could this be? He, too, had been called to the feast. He, too, was at the marriage in Cana of Galilee....
“Yes, my dear, I too am called, called and invited,” he heard a soft voice say close above him. “Why have you hidden yourself here, out of sight? Come and join us.”
That was his voice, Father Zossima’s voice. And it had to be him, since he was the one calling!
The elder took Alyosha’s hand, and Alyosha rose from his knees.

“We are rejoicing,” the little, thin old man went on. “We are drinking the new wine, the wine of a new and great gladness. Do you see how many guests there are? Here are the bride and the bridegroom, and here is the wise governor of the feast, tasting the new wine. Why are you surprised to see me? I gave an onion to a beggar, and so I am here, too. And many here have given just one onion each, only one little onion.... What are all our deeds? And you, my gentle one, you, my kind boy, you also knew how to give an onion to a starving woman today. Begin your work, dear one, begin it, gentle one!... Do you see our Sun? Do you see Him?”
“I am afraid ... I dare not look,” whispered Alyosha.

“Do not be afraid of Him. He is terrible in His greatness and awesome in His majesty, but infinitely merciful. Out of love He became like us, and He rejoices with us. He is turning the water into wine so that the guests’ gladness will not be cut short. He is waiting for new guests, He is calling new ones without ceasing, for ever and ever.... Look, they are bringing more wine. Do you see? They are bringing the vessels....”
Something glowed in Alyosha’s heart, something filled it until it ached, and tears of rapture rose up from his soul.... He stretched out his hands, gave a cry and woke.

There was the coffin again, and the open window, and the soft, solemn, clear reading of the Gospel. But Alyosha did not hear the reading. It was strange: he had fallen asleep on his knees, and now he was on his feet. Suddenly, as if something had thrown him forward, he took three firm, quick steps right up to the coffin. His shoulder brushed Father Païssy, and he did not notice. Father Païssy looked up from his book for an instant, then looked away at once, seeing that something strange was happening to the boy. For half a minute Alyosha gazed at the coffin, at the covered, motionless dead man lying in it, with the ikon on his chest and the peaked cap with the eight-pointed cross on his head. He had only just heard that voice, and it was still ringing in his ears. He stood listening, still expecting more words, but then he suddenly turned sharply and walked out of the cell.

He did not stop on the steps, either, but hurried down them. His soul, brimming with rapture, craved freedom, space and open air. Above him the vault of heaven stretched vast and fathomless, full of soft, shining stars. The Milky Way ran in two pale streams from the zenith to the horizon. The night was fresh, still and motionless, and it wrapped the earth. The white towers and golden domes of the cathedral stood out against the sapphire sky. The gorgeous autumn flowers in the beds around the house were asleep until morning. The silence of the earth seemed to melt into the silence of the heavens. The mystery of the earth joined with the mystery of the stars....

Alyosha stood and gazed, and then he suddenly flung himself down on the ground. He did not know why he was embracing it. He could not have said why he longed so irresistibly to kiss it, to kiss all of it. But he kissed it, weeping and sobbing and soaking it with his tears, and he vowed passionately to love it, to love it for ever and ever. “Water the earth with the tears of your joy and love those tears,” echoed in his soul.
What was he weeping over?

Oh! In his rapture he wept even over the stars that shone down on him from the abyss of space, and “he was not ashamed of that ecstasy.” It was as if threads ran from all those countless worlds of God and tied his soul to them, and his soul trembled all over “in contact with other worlds.” He longed to forgive everyone for everything, and to ask forgiveness. Oh, not for himself, but for all people, for all and for everything. “And others are praying for me, too,” echoed again in his soul. But with every moment he felt plainly, almost tangibly, that something as firm and unshakable as that vault of heaven was entering his soul. It was as if some idea had seized the sovereignty of his mind—and for all his life, for ever and ever. He had fallen to the earth a weak boy, and he rose up a resolute fighter, and he knew and felt it suddenly, at the very moment of his ecstasy. And never, never in all his life would Alyosha forget that minute.
“Someone visited my soul in that hour,” he would say later, believing every word.
Three days later he left the monastery, in keeping with the words of his elder, who had told him to “sojourn in the world.”
